methods.name: claim
methods.doc: Takes the earliest item that is due, and marks it as being worked on so a second worker cannot take it too. Returns null when nothing is due, which is different from the queue being empty.

methods.name: release
methods.doc: Puts a claimed item back, for a worker that could not finish it.

methods.name: promote
methods.doc: Brings every look at one piece of work that is still held back forward to now, and says how many moved.

methods.name: recover
methods.doc: Returns items abandoned by a dead worker so they get picked up again.

methods.name: prune
methods.doc: Deletes finished items past their retention, so the directory stays small.

methods.name: watch
methods.doc: Calls back as soon as a stop is requested, and returns the function that stops watching.

plans.doc: Do the work, stay in this state, and look again straight away. The next look sees whatever the actions recorded, which is how a pure decision function drives work that takes minutes or hours.

skills.name: amy
skills.description: Drive amy, the machine that walks a work ticket from the tracker's working status to a QA handoff, and turns friction it hits into a plan in the repository that friction is about.

skills.name: amy-btw
skills.description: Capture something said in passing as work amy will actually do — "btw the deps in the api are stale", "also check whether that monitor is still firing" — without opening a ticket and without leaving what you are doing.

skills.name: amy-init
skills.description: Set amy up on this machine end to end — the state directory, the config, the roster, the plugins it needs installed, the credentials, the notification channel — by reading what is already here and asking only what the machine cannot answer.

skills.name: amy-show-me
skills.description: Show what an amy workflow is and where its work has got to, visually — the state machine, the path one piece of work took, what is waiting on what.

skills.name: amy-status
skills.description: Answer "where is my work" from the project's side rather than the machine's — what is open, what amy is working on right now, what is waiting on you, what is stuck — across every workflow at once, as a page you can keep open.

skills.name: amy-workflow
skills.description: Design a new amy workflow, or change one that exists, by being interrogated one question at a time until the shape is settled — then write it as its own package.

shipped.name: @amykit/agent-kit
shipped.description: What every agent does the same way: the prompts, the git dance, and the JSON.

shipped.name: @amykit/cli
shipped.description: The amy command line: one install per machine, reached from any harness.

shipped.name: @amykit/core
shipped.description: Plugin contracts, the action catalogue, the registry and the loader. Knows no domain.

shipped.name: @amykit/model-specs
shipped.description: What each model costs per token, vendored and versioned.

shipped.name: @amykit/plugin-agent-relay
shipped.description: One agent made of several: swaps harness on a quota, escalates model on a failure.

settings.name: budget
settings.description: what the agents may spend, per window: perFiveHours and perWeek, each with tokens and/or costUsd, plus stopAt, the fraction of a ceiling at which new work stops being started

settings.name: ladder
settings.description: the contributed agents to try, in order, such as [claude:sonnet, claude:opus, codex:gpt-5]. Empty means every contributed agent, in the order the plugins were mounted

settings.name: ladderByStep
settings.description: a ladder for one step, overriding the one above, keyed by the workflow's action name: {"triage": ["claude:haiku"], "implement": ["claude:opus"]}. Reading a ticket and writing the change are not the same job, and one list for both means paying the expensive model to do the cheap step

settings.name: skillRoots
settings.description: where installed skills are looked for. Empty means ~/.claude/skills, which is where the harness looks

settings.name: skills
settings.description: which skills answer for a step, in the order they are tried, keyed by the workflow's action name: {"triage": ["/logion"]}. A skill named here must be installed, or the mount is refused

shipped.name: @amykit/plugin-claude
shipped.description: The claude CLI as the agent, with git on the side.

settings.name: defaultBranch
settings.description: the branch new work is cut from, which is not always `main`

settings.name: model
settings.description: passed to the CLI as --model, which is the flag it accepts

settings.name: models
settings.description: the model tiers to offer the relay, cheapest first. One agent is contributed per tier, named `claude:<model>`. Empty means a single agent using `model`

settings.name: reviewerHints
settings.description: guidance appended when answering a particular reviewer, by host login

settings.name: timeoutMs
settings.description: how long one agent call may run before it is given up on

rules.title: The core imports no workflow and no plugin
Error types live in one canonical module per domain
Private and generated modules are not imported across the boundary
A comment block stays under the line ceiling
No function exceeds the cyclomatic ceiling
Every suppression names a code and a reason
The untyped escape hatch is banned, and the message names the alternative
A skipped or expected-to-fail test says why
A released rule never gets weaker than the version this repository locked
Dependency manifests move only with an explicit lock update
Regenerating the derived artifacts changes nothing
The guardrail's own configuration is hash-locked
Generated artifacts are hash-locked and not hand-edited
Every frozen exception carries a future review date
The guardrail may be strengthened, never quietly weakened
A gate requires every check its plan's criteria name
A gate activated by touched paths needs digest-verified, non-stale evidence
Every marked promise names the gate that proves it
Repo-relative documentation links resolve
Every enabled rule is cited in prose, and every citation resolves
Every acceptance criterion names the check that proves it
Every plan declares its exit condition and sits in the execution order
New top-level files are declared before they appear
Every command a rule's prose quotes is one this `sf` accepts
Every enabled rule has a mutation that proves it fires
An enabled rule must be capable of producing a finding
Concurrent code is exercised under a race detector
rules.reason: there is no dynamic race detector for this language, and the rule names none. One process, one event loop, and the one thing that is genuinely concurrent — two workers on one queue — is settled by an atomic rename rather than by a lock, and proven by the file-queue gate.

rules.title: Something detects code nothing reaches
Something audits dependencies for known vulnerabilities
An address in a fixture belongs to nobody
Something scans the code for known-insecure patterns
Nothing blocks while a lock is held
rules.reason: the rule has no query for TypeScript, so enabling it here would be a rule that cannot fire. Nothing in this workspace takes a lock; the queue is a directory and claiming is a rename.

rules.title: A function does not acquire a second lock while holding the first
rules.reason: same reason as the rule above. No TypeScript query, and no locks to hold.

rules.title: Something would notice the code getting slower
Something scans for committed secrets
Something scans the CI workflows themselves
